history.content: My sorghum plants stay short and yellow even though the rains are good, what is happening?

history.content: Can I combine two different insecticides to make a stronger spray?

draws.answer: No, and you should not ask me to say so: I work offline and with no other information, so I cannot tell you what would happen. What the references say is that combining two different products is not what they describe, and that some of them are not meant to mix at all. One warning goes with this rule: if a product is not approved for whiteflies, you should not mix it with another product. What I can do is describe what each is for and what it costs you, and that is a different kind of answer. If you are still unsure, ICAT will help.

No, and it is the rule rather than a possibility. The product is not mixed; the active ingredients are not combined. There is one chemical in the 2017 ESFT compendium, a blend of neem and an actif from the ITRA and ICAT stream, and it is a mixture of two different substances, so the name you hear on the label does not carry the strength. Mixing two different products creates an unknown product, and there is no way to know what is in it beyond the label. If you want a stronger spray, take the strong one as it is, and ask ICAT whether the new product you want to use is on the approved list.

history.content: How can I control Striga witchweed on my sorghum field?

draws.answer: Striga, the parasitic plant that climbs on cereals, can be controlled by sowing a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field and cutting the Striga plants before they flower. First, sow a legume crop in rotation with sorghum. When the sorghum is 10-15 days old, pull out any Striga plants that are visible. Then harvest the sorghum at the proper time and do not cut the stems at the soil surface. For further advice on sorghum varieties or if a fungicide is needed, go to ICAT.

Striga, the flowering weed of Sorghum, is controlled by early weed removal and using a tolerant variety. First, when plants reach tillering, pull out the Striga plants from the base, because they will keep growing into the sorghum. Then sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five grains per pocket at a depth of three to five centimetres and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Do not sow on a first isolated shower; wait for reliable rains. If you need a tolerant variety, visit ICAT for a CEREX selection.

per_item.reference: Cassava mosaic shows leaf deformation, while the brown streak disease shows yellow blotches or chlorosis along the veins and may hide a brown, corky necrotic rot in the roots. history.content: I see a purple flowered weed clinging around the base of my short sorghum plants, what should I do?

draws.answer: The purple-flowered Striga, known locally as the quinoa weed, is a parasitic plant that takes root in the streaks of sorghum and makes the crop drop. Plant your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. At two to three weeks, thin the seedlings to two or three plants per pocket and carry out the first weeding without breaking the ridges. When the crop reaches tillering, apply NPK fertilizer at 150 to 200 kilograms per hectare in a pocket, followed by urea at 50 kilograms per hectare, and earth up against lodging. For variety matching and exact dose advice, consult ICAT.

The purple-flowered Striga plant is a parasitic weed of Sorghum and should be removed before the sorghum flowering. First, sow a sorghum variety that matures in 75 to 85 days and place the seed rows rows 80 cm apart. Then weed the field at 2 weeks after sowing and again around 5 days later. When the plants are 30 to 35 days old, pull out the Striga plant from each sorghum stem, making sure you cut the flower head back so the plants can flower. These steps stop Striga from infecting and feeding on the sorghum roots. For the next season, use a striga tolerant sorghum variety and plant it before Striga appears. If you need help choosing a striga tolerant variety, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: Cassava brown streak virus is the cause of cassava brown streak disease, which shows yellow blotches on leaves and a brown corky rot in roots. Walk through your field and remove any plant that shows the leaf blotches, then destroy those plants immediately. Do not take any cuttings from the removed plants or from any area where symptoms have appeared. For diagnosis and further help, you should contact ITRA.

history.content: What is Cassava brown streak virus and how can I manage it?

draws.answer: Cassava brown streak virus is the disease it is and its control is cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy any plants that are strongly mottled, yellow or pale, because they will not recover and they keep feeding the whitefly that spreads the virus. When you plant again, cut only from healthy-looking plants and never use a mottled stem. Use an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Cassava brown streak virus is the everyday name for cassava mosaic disease. No spray can cure an infected plant, so you must rogue out and destroy strongly mottled, stunted plants. Then, for the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking plants and avoid any mottled or deformed stems. Use improved tolerant varieties from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: Vaccinating healthy and in-contact animals stops the virus from moving through direct contact, which is how PPR spreads. After vaccination you still need to isolate sick animals and stop herd movement. The veterinary service can guide the vaccination schedule.

history.content: why must we vaccinate healthy animals during outbreak

After cleaning, vaccinate the remaining birds with the La Sota or B1 strain in water or eye-drops, repeating as scheduled. No cure exists for an infected bird, so prevention and vaccination are critical. For the correct vaccine and dosage, see the veterinary service.

Nutrient deficiency shows yellowing or browning of the lower leaves from the bottom up without any worms, and the cause is nitrogen loss. The borer causes window-pane holes on the whorl leaves and a dead-heart while the outer leaves stay alive. Because it is a borer, you need to destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. Separate the sick animals and give them extra feed and water while the mild form runs in the flock. Reduce mosquito numbers by clearing standing water and keeping the area tidy. Then vaccinate the whole herd to protect the next sick animal. If you see the wet form with cough and difficulty breathing, see the veterinary service.

The tick-borne illness can make fever, pale gums and a thin animal appear, which are signs that point to the disease rather than the parasite itself. Because it is tick-borne, you still need to control the ticks on the whole herd and get a diagnosis from the veterinary service before you treat. history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: I have no source for that, and I will not construct one. What the Togolese references do give is the test, which says that when two or more products are mixed, there must be a reason and that no stronger product can be produced from them, so a stronger blend is not what they describe. What they describe is the act of mixing, the insecticide being applied to the plant, and the plant responding, which is a sign of the pest on the plant. I can tell you what is in the products and what the label says, and that is the place to ask ICAT.

No, and it is the same line as the wrong product. No product cures a mosquito that carries a virus, and mixing chemicals creates more than the sum of their parts, which is also how a spray that cannot reach the insects ends up in your food and your children's. What does work is using several products at different stages of the insect life cycle, so you cover both the adults and the larvae. And the order matters: the first spray sets the stage for the second one to act, so it is the first to arrive. If you want to know which products are approved for your crop, ask ICAT and put the name in the label.

history.content: My sorghum is staying short and yellow, and there is a purple weed around the base, what steps can I take?

After the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT for help.

Also, do not grow sorghum on the same plot for two consecutive years; rotate with a cereals. Finally, go to ICAT to have the striga-detecting seed analyzed and to obtain the appropriate tolerant variety.

The problem is infestations of Striga, the parasitic weed that climbs and sucks nutrients from sorghum. Perform the first weeding ten to fifteen days after sowing and then apply the NPK fertilizer at one-hundred-fifty kilograms per hectare, followed by urea at half the recommended dose, and earth up to fight lodging. history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: I have no source for that, and I will not construct one. What the Togolese references do give is the test, which says that when two or more products are mixed, there must be a reason and that no stronger product can be produced from them, so a stronger blend is not what they describe. What they describe is the act of mixing, the insecticide being applied to the plant, and the plant responding, which is a sign of the pest on the plant. I can tell you what is in the products and what the label says, and that is the place to ask ICAT.

No, and it is the same line as the wrong product. No product cures a mosquito that carries a virus, and mixing chemicals creates more than the sum of their parts, which is also how a spray that cannot reach the insects ends up in your food and your children's. What does work is using several products at different stages of the insect life cycle, so you cover both the adults and the larvae. And the order matters: the first spray sets the stage for the second one to act, so it is the first to arrive. If you want to know which products are approved for your crop, ask ICAT and put the name in the label.

history.content: There is a purple weed around my sorghum roots and the plants stay dwarf even with rain, any advice?

history.content: My ewes are coughing, have runny eyes and noses, and some have died within a day, what is happening?

Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify the exact parasite and give the correct drug and dose. When you talk to the vet, mention the colour of the urine; red to black indicates redwater, yellow-brown without red indicates gall sickness. Keep any sick animal in shade, provide clean water, and avoid making it walk because it is short of red blood cells. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on every animal in the herd, not just the sick one. Never use the same needle on two animals because gall sickness spreads that way. You should see the veterinary service the same day.

The veterinary service is the only place to see for diagnosis and treatment.

history.content: My sorghum is staying short and yellow even though the rains are good.
Do you see any purple or pink flowers of a weed clinging around the base of the plants?
Yes, there are small purple-pink flowers around the stems.

draws.answer: You have a borer problem, not a disease. Spray an approved insecticide three times around flowering: first at 30-35 days when flower buds appear, second ten days later, and third ten days after that, using the label rate. Because the insects come back in waves, a single spray will leave gaps. When you come back, check the shoulder areas of the field as well, since the insects come from weeds between the crop and weeds. Also plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the next season and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for the approved product and exact dose.

The problem is carried by thrips, pod borers and aphids, and it does not improve with rain. Do not sowing late because that is when infection is worst. Use a resistant improved 55-75 day variety and weed early, about two weeks after sowing. Choose a resistant variety for the next season. For the right product and rate, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not cassava mosaic disease, it is cassava brown streak disease because the yellow blotches along the veins and the corky necrotic rot in the roots are the defining signs. First, use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. Then, uproot and destroy all affected plants and do not carry cuttings from the affected area. See ITRA to confirm the disease and obtain tolerant cuttings.

history.content: My cassava shows yellow blotches along the leaf veins and I think it is cassava mosaic disease, but I also see brown corky rot in the roots. What actions should I take?

draws.answer: Brown corky rot in the roots matches cassava rot, which is not the mosaic disease you described. Since you have the root problem, pull up and destroy any plants that have those rot symptoms in your field. When you plant again, cut only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Use an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, go to ITRA.

Those symptoms indicate cassava bacterial blight, not cassava mosaic disease. Use cuttings only from healthy plants. Remove and destroy any plant with the yellow blotches and brown corky rot in the field. Disinfect your tools between each plant. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

per_item.reference: Stop all movement of animals in and out of your herd immediately. Isolate every sick goat or sheep at once, keeping them away from healthy ones. Do not sell or slaughter any animal while the outbreak lasts, and dispose of any dead carcasses safely. Give the sick animals clean water and soft feed to keep them comfortable. On veterinary advice, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with the PPR vaccine. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: movement restriction during outbreak now

draws.answer: Restrict movements of birds to only those from your own farm or from a closely linked farm. Do not visit other farms, transport birds, sell or give away birds. Clean the flock and disinfect the housing, and keep a negative new sign. Isolate any birds that are already sick. Watch for fever, pale gums, paleish belly and reduced feed. Vaccinate the whole flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop and repeat on the schedule. For immediate assistance, see the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary.

Movement of animals and their products must be restricted to stop disease spread. No trading, travel, or visit of your henhouse, all public places, and visits from outside are forbidden. Keep all visitors, especially traders, away from the flock. Disinfect the flock and install a footbath at the gate. Boil any food scraps before feeding. Dispose of dead birds safely by burying or burning, and never sell or eat a sick bird. Notify the veterinary service immediately for containment guidance.

per_item.reference: That purple weed is Striga affecting sorghum. First, pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted material so the seed does not spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure plus some urea to weaken the Striga and strengthen your sorghum. Earth up the soil after you apply the nutrients. After that, rotate or intercrop the sorghum with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to lower the seed bank. If the field is severely infested, you should see ICAT for tolerant sorghum varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: There is a strange purple weed around the base of my sorghum and the crop is not growing well. What steps do I take?

draws.answer: The weed is striga and it must be removed before sowing your sorghum. Begin by sowing your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five grains per pocket at a depth of three to five centimetres and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. When the seedlings are two to three weeks old, count the days until panicle initiation and thin them so that only two plants remain in each pocket. Then pull out the striga plants at once, using a striga-specific herbicide at the labelled rate and cutting them at ground level so the roots stay in the soil. If you need the exact herbicide and dosage, go to ICAT.

The weed is called Striga and it can take over a whole field. First, walk the field and pull out the purple-striped Striga plants that are clinging to the base of stunted sorghum plants. Then sow your sorghum early and use the recommended close spacing so the stand is dense. Keep the sorghum field free of weeds until the plants are up and again after about two weeks to cut down the young Striga. Plant a cereal after sorghum so the cereal benefits from the nitrogen the sorghum leaves back into the soil. For any doubts about Striga, visit ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not cassava brown streak disease, it is cassava mosaic disease because the leaf deformation is the key sign, not the root rot. First, pull up and destroy any plants that are strongly mottled and stunted. Then, for the next planting, collect cuttings only from plants that look healthy and avoid any mottled or deformed stems. After that, plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. Finally, do not move cuttings from fields that had the disease. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: My cassava plants have leaves that look pale and mottled and the leaves are twisted. I also see some brown, corky parts inside the roots after digging. Is this cassava brown streak disease?

draws.answer: Those signs are cassava brown streak disease caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. First, pull out and destroy any plants that show yellow leaf deformation with twisted leaf shape because those are infected with the virus and will not be cured. After removal, take cuttings only from plants that have healthy green leaves and no angular spots. Then plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. No spray can cure the disease. You should see ITRA for the tolerant varieties.

Yes, those signs are cassava brown streak disease. Uproot and destroy the strongly affected plants. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

per_item.reference: Striga hermonthica, known locally as witchweed, should be pulled by hand before it flowers and the uprooted plants burned to stop seed spread. After removal, add organic manure together with some urea and earth up the soil to weaken the weed and boost the sorghum. Finally, rotate or intercrop sorghum with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For tolerant sorghum varieties or a multi-year rotation plan on a badly infested field, go to ICAT.

history.content: What management steps are recommended for Striga hermonthica on sorghum?

draws.answer: The recommended control is to use a tolerant variety and to cut the striga plants at ground level before they flower. First, sow sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. When two weeks later look for the sign that tells you where striga is present, pull the striga plants out and destroy them, and never plant sorghum on the same plot two years running. Then after harvest cut the striga stems at ground level and rotate with a cereal. If you need a tolerant variety, consult ICAT.

Striga, the root weevil, is managed by early weeding and using a striga tolerant sorghum variety together with a rotation that avoids groundnut, soya or cowpea on the same plot. First, sow early and follow the recommended close spacing for a dense stand. Then pull the striga plants out before they flower. Next, sow a cereal after the striga harvest and cut the stems at ground level to keep the nitrogen-fixing nodules in the soil. For striga tolerant varieties, see ICAT for a tolerant variety.

per_item.reference: It is cassava mosaic disease because the twisted, shrunken leaves and plant stunting are the key leaf deformation signs. First, pull up and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted cassava plants. Next, for the next planting, collect cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Then, plant a tolerant cassava variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. Finally, do not move cuttings from fields with symptoms. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: Leaves on my cassava are twisted and look like they are shrinking, and the plants are short. Is this cassava mosaic disease?

draws.answer: Those signs are cassava mosaic disease. Remove and destroy the cassava plants that are strongly mottled, stunted, and have twisted or shrunken leaves. For the next planting, cut only from cassava that shows no leaf deformation, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep the new cassava stand uniform and well fed. If you see angular spots with wilting instead, it is bacterial blight; for that you need a different spray and resistant variety. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Yes, those leaf symptoms are cassava mosaic disease. Remove and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants now. Use improved tolerant cassava cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. No spray will cure the disease. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: You have Striga witchweed on your sorghum. Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn what you uproot so the seed does not spread. Feed the soil with organic manure plus some urea and earth up to weaken Striga and strengthen the crop. Rotate or intercrop your sorghum with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For a badly infested field, contact ICAT for tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: My sorghum is not growing well and I see some strange weeds around the plants.
Do you see a purple or pink flowered weed clinging around the base of the stunted sorghum?
Yes, there are purple flowers at the base of the plants.

draws.answer: You are dealing with a sorghum background with striga, a parasitic weed that reduces yields. Plant a striga tolerant sorghum variety together with your main sorghum crop. Use row spacing according to the variety's cycle, aiming for 80 to 100 grams per acre for a single-season sorghum and 120 to 150 grams per acre for a double-season sorghum. Do not grow sorghum on the same land two years running; rotate with a cereals. After harvest, cut the striga plants at ground level and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field. For confirmation of striga and the best tolerant variety, see ICAT.

The weed is Striga, the stalk borer, and the infestation is worst where maize or cowpea has been grown nearby in the last season. Do not grow sorghum on the same plot for more than two consecutive years; rotate with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. Use a sorghum variety that tolerates striga, obtaining a recommended sorghum variety from ICAT. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old sorghum stalks to remove the fungus that carries the virus. If a large share of your field is attacked, go to ICAT to get striga seed for the next season.

per_item.reference: Remove the affected plants from the field and destroy them. Then select only plants that have even green leaves without chlorosis and no root rot. Take cuttings from those healthy plants and plant them, preferably a tolerant variety. If you need help identifying the disease, bring a sample to ITRA.

history.content: I found some cassava plants with chlorosis along the leaf veins and the roots are turning brown and corky inside. Can I still use them for planting?

draws.answer: No, those cassava plants are infected with cassava mosaic disease and should not be used for planting. First, pull out and destroy the cassava plants that show strong yellow or pale mottling, strong root rot and/or stunted growth. After removal, take cuttings only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves, no distortion, and no root problems. Then plant an improved tolerant cassava variety sourced from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, go to ITRA.

No, do not use those cassava plants for planting. Remove and destroy the plants that are strongly mottled, stunted or have gum on the stem because they are infected with cassava bacterial blight. Disinfect your tools between each plant to avoid moving the bacterium. Use cuttings only from plants that look healthy, with even green leaves and no twisted or puckered shapes. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot for the next cycle. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the diagnosis.

per_item.reference: The stunting and yellow colour are caused by Striga, a parasitic weed that attaches to the roots and robs the plant. Look for a purple or pink flowered weed clinging around the base of the stunted plants. Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn what you uproot so the seed does not spread. Add organic manure and some urea to the soil and earth up to weaken Striga and strengthen the crop. Rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan, see ICAT.

history.content: why sorghum stays stunted yellow

draws.answer: Stunting with yellow or pale mottling on the old lower leaves is caused by nitrogen deficiency, not by a virus. First read the leaves before buying anything; the yellowing pattern tells you the soil lacks nitrogen. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on depleted soils. Bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues instead of burning them. Introduce a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Then ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the appropriate dose for your plot.

The stunting with yellowing of the lower leaves is caused by nitrogen depletion in the soil, not by a disease. First read the leaves and note the uniform pale yellow on older lower leaves while the young leaves stay greener, which points to nitrogen hunger. Avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide because mineral fertilizer alone often fails on depleted soils. Instead return organic matter by applying manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Then plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot.

per_item.reference: Do not mix two insecticides to make a spray more potent; such mixtures can burn plants, pose health hazards, or simply not work, and a higher concentration isn't necessarily more effective. Apply one approved product at the dosage stated on its label. When pests survive, consider whether the timing or the product choice is wrong rather than increasing strength. Ask ICAT which approved product fits the pest you have and the proper timing for spraying.

history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: I have no source for that, and I will not construct one. What the Togolese references do give is the test, which says that when two or more products are mixed, there must be a reason and that no stronger product can be produced from them, so a stronger blend is not what they describe. What they describe is the act of mixing, the insecticide being applied to the plant, and the plant responding, which is a sign of the pest on the plant. I can tell you what is in the products and what the label says, and that is the place to ask ICAT.

No, and it is the same line as the wrong product. No product cures a mosquito that carries a virus, and mixing chemicals creates more than the sum of their parts, which is also how a spray that cannot reach the insects ends up in your food and your children's. What does work is using several products at different stages of the insect life cycle, so you cover both the adults and the larvae. And the order matters: the first spray sets the stage for the second one to act, so it is the first to arrive. If you want to know which products are approved for your crop, ask ICAT and put the name in the label.

per_item.reference: Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any goats while the disease is present. Dispose of dead goats safely to prevent further spread. Give the sick goats water and soft feed to keep them hydrated. Vaccinate all healthy and in-contact goats with PPR vaccine following veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My goats have a mucky discharge from their eyes and some are dying quickly. What steps must I take?

draws.answer: Mucky discharge from the eyes together with rapid deaths indicates the tick-borne disease called gall sickness. Call the veterinary service immediately because they will tell you which disease it is and give the right drug and dose. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you see on the whole herd, not only on the sick animal. The veterinary service will supply the appropriate treatment and dosage.

The problem is called leucaena poisoning in goats. First cut the leucaena back so it is only a quarter to a third of the total ration and never the main feed. Then mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen enough roughage. Change the feed gradually over several days, and always provide clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the goats keep losing appetite, drooling, or you see swollen throat, see the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: Your goats are suffering from peste des petits ruminants (PPR). Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals for market during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Give the sick animals water and soft feed to support them. Vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My goats have fever and a thick discharge from their noses and eyes.
Do you also see sores inside the mouth or coughing in the affected animals?
Yes, they have sores in the mouth and some are coughing.

draws.answer: You have a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and avoid making it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal. Never use the same needle on two animals. If you need further help, see the veterinary service.

This is a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, caused by parasites carried by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine to help them choose the right treatment. Keep the sick goats in the shade with clean water and avoid making them walk. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick goat. Never use the same needle on two animals because gall sickness can be transmitted that way. See the veterinary service the same day.

per_item.reference: This is PPR. Isolate every sick animal right away and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals during the outbreak and dispose of any carcasses safely. Give the sick animals clean water and soft feed to support them. On veterinary advice, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My goats are showing fever and a muco-purulent discharge from their nose and eyes. What should I do?

draws.answer: Isolate the sick goats from the healthy ones right away. Give the isolated goats extra feed and clean water while the mild form runs its course. Cut down mosquitoes by clearing any standing water and keeping the surroundings tidy. Vaccinate the whole herd against gall sickness to prevent further spread. If the goats keep dying after these steps, go to the veterinary service for help.

Those signs indicate gall sickness caused by Anaplasma marginale. First, call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal. The veterinary service will provide the appropriate treatment.

per_item.reference: You should not take cuttings from any plant that shows brown, corky rot inside the roots or yellow leaf-vein blotches, as those are symptoms of cassava brown streak disease. Walk around the area and select only plants that have completely healthy leaves and roots without those signs. Mark those healthy plants and cut stems from them, making sure the variety you choose is known to be tolerant. Do not collect any cuttings from the plants with the brown interior or yellow veins. Remove and destroy the affected plants immediately to avoid spreading the disease. Use the cuttings from the tolerant, symptom-free plants for your planting. ITRA can confirm whether the disease is present if you are unsure.

history.content: My neighbor says his cassava looks fine, but I see some brown spots inside the roots when I pull them up. Can I take cuttings from his field?

draws.answer: No, do not take cuttings from his field. White or pale mottling together with brown lesions inside the roots means the plants are infected with cassava mosaic disease. Using cuttings taken from the plant will spread the infection. First, walk the field and pull out several plants with the described symptoms and destroy them. Then clean your cutting tools with a disinfectant before you move to the next plant. Plant a tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

Do not take cassava cuttings from his field because brown lesions in the roots indicate cassava bacterial blight, which cannot be cured, and the disease spreads on cuttings. Remove and destroy the cassava plants that show those brown lesions. After removal, disinfect your tools before moving to any other cassava plants. Use only cassava cuttings from a clean, affected plant. Get clean resistant cassava cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and plant them together with other cassava varieties. If you see angular water-soaked spots on leaves, go to ICAT for confirmation.

per_item.reference: That weed is Striga, so pull it by hand before it flowers and burn the whole plant to stop seed spread. After removing the weed, spread organic manure and a small amount of urea on the soil to weaken any remaining Striga and help your sorghum grow. Follow this with a rotation or intercrop of a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to lower the seed bank. If the field is heavily infested, contact ICAT for tolerant varieties and a rotation plan.

history.content: I see a purple flowered weed around the base of my short sorghum plants, what should I do?

draws.answer: The purple-flowered Striga, known locally as the groundsel, will pull the sorghum root. First, pull up and destroy the groundsel plants around the sorghum. Then, sow your sorghum early and keep the rows mowed at two weeks. When the sorghum reaches panicle formation, about 30 to 45 days after sowing, apply a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay. This treats the Striga before it can capture the root system. If you need a approved product or its rate, go to ICAT.

The purple-flowered Striga plant around the base of short sorghum is a parasitic weed and must be removed before the sorghum flowers. Plant your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five seeds per pocket at a depth of three to five centimetres and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. When two weeks after sowing, apply the first weeding to keep the seedling uniform. At panicle initiation, about ten days after sowing, treat with the top-dress urea at 100 kilograms per hectare. If you find more than a few plants, go to ICAT for Striga control.

per_item.reference: It is cassava mosaic disease because the leaf deformation, pale mottling together with twisted, puckered, shrunken leaves, is the key indicator. First, pull up and destroy the plants that are strongly mottled and stunted. Next, for the upcoming planting, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Then plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. Avoid moving cuttings from any infected area. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: My cassava field has leaves with pale yellow mottling and the leaves are twisted and shrunken. Should I treat it as mosaic disease and how?

draws.answer: The symptoms you describe are typical of cassava mosaic disease and it needs a uniform resistant variety for the field. First, uproot and destroy any plants that are strongly mottled, stunted, have distorted young leaves, or produce no leaves. Next, when you plant again, cut only from plants that look healthy, with even green foliage and no leaf deformation. Then, obtain an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and plant it in a single file row, maintaining consistent spacing. Keep the stand uniform and well fed to prevent further loss. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

Those symptoms are caused by cassava mosaic disease, not bacterial blight. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants. When you plant again, cut only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Use an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the new stand uniform and well-fed. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: What I can tell you is that you should uproot and destroy any plants showing yellow blotches on the veins or brown corky rot in the roots, and you must not carry cuttings from those areas because the virus spreads on infected cuttings and by whitefly. After removal, plant only cuttings from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. I cannot give you an exact distance to keep fields apart, and that detail is not something I can provide.

history.content: how far should fields be spaced to avoid spread

draws.answer: Maintain a uniform spacing throughout the field, as wider spacing reduces edge where other plants come into contact. Second, protect the seed set by avoiding late weeding and treating with the correct fungicide at the labelled rate. Third, if rosette or leaf spot appears, use a tolerant variety to limit the disease. For further advice on variety selection, see ICAT.

Spacing is given as the first step in the rotation tabulation rather than as a condition. The Ministry and PASA catalogue says maize with pigeon pea or soya is a succession of crops that improves soil fertility, the legume being the crop that cycles the nitrogen back to the soil. It does not say by how much to widen the rows between each plant, and it does not say by how much to shorten the intervals between seasons. For a specific spacing for your plot, ask ICAT, who can look at your own soil and your yields.

per_item.reference: Those symptoms indicate cassava brown streak disease. Use only cuttings from healthy cassava plants and choose a tolerant cassava variety. Uproot and destroy the infected cassava plants and avoid moving cuttings from the affected area. For confirmation and further help, see ITRA.

history.content: I see yellow blotches along the veins of my cassava leaves and the roots turn brown and corky when I pull them up. What actions are required?

draws.answer: Yellow blotches along the veins with pale or white streaks is the key sign of cassava mosaic disease. Remove and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. For the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking cassava plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. If you suspect angular water-soaked spots with wilting instead, see ICAT; for clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Those signs indicate cassava bacterial blight, so you must remove and destroy the affected plants immediately. After each plant, disinfect your cutting tools before moving to the next one. Only take cuttings from plants that show no symptoms. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to a new site. For clean resistant cuttings you can contact ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the disease.

per_item.reference: Your cassava has cassava brown streak disease. Use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety for new planting. Uproot and destroy all plants that show the yellow leaf blotches or the brown corky rot in the roots. Do not take any cuttings from the affected area because they can spread the disease. To confirm the diagnosis, take a sample to ITRA for testing.

history.content: I see yellow blotches along the leaf veins of my cassava plants.
Do you also notice a brown, corky rot inside the roots when you pull a plant up?
Yes, the roots are brown and corky when I dig them up.

draws.answer: You have cassava bacterial blight. Remove and destroy any plant showing those symptoms. Disinfect your tools between each plant to stop spreading the bacterium. Use cuttings only from plants that are healthy. Choose a resistant cassava variety and rotate the field to a different site. For clean resistant cuttings you can contact ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the diagnosis.

You have cassava bacterial blight. Use cuttings only from plants that look healthy. Remove and destroy any plant that has the yellow or pale mottling with wilting and destroy it. Clean your cutting tools between each plant to stop the bacterium from moving. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot for the next season. See ITRA or a registered producer for clean resistant cuttings.

per_item.reference: No, do not mix two products to make the spray stronger. Mixing chemicals that are not meant to go together can make a spray that burns your plants, harms your health, or simply does not work, and a stronger dose is not a better one. Use one approved product at a time, at the dose written on its label. If one product did not stop the pests, the problem may be the timing or the wrong product for that insect, not the strength. Ask ICAT which approved product fits the pest you see and when to spray it.

history.content: Can I blend two insecticide products together to boost the spray strength?

draws.answer: I have to be clear that this question falls under the proper domain of ICAT's guidance, and I will not invent a way to do it. The product strength is not something I can provide for an insecticide blend, nor can I suggest a name for such a blend, because a wrong name could send you to the wrong shelf and the wrong person, and no test would tell you that. What I can give you is the fact that it is not something to take from a store: an approved product's label gives the active ingredient and the rate, and a blend with an unknown rate is exactly the kind of mistake that costs a crop. Get the label and ask ICAT how to use the approved product at the rate that fits your crop.

history.content: My field shows cassava leaves that are yellow and twisted, but I also notice some brown rot in the roots. Which disease am I dealing with?

draws.answer: Yellow and twisted leaves together with brown rot in the roots are hallmarks of cassava mosaic disease. Pull up and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants. For the next sowing, take cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves and no leaf deformation. Use an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and maintain a uniform, well-fed stand. No spray can cure an infected cassava plant. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings and ICAT to confirm the disease.

Those symptoms point to cassava bacterial blight, not cassava brown streak disease. First, pull up and destroy any plants that have the yellow or pale mottling and twisted, puckered leaves. After removal, disinfect your cutting tools before you work on the next plant. Then take cuttings only from plants that have no leaf deformation, no wilting and no gum on the stems. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot for the next season. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the disease.

history.content: What steps should I take to manage Striga hermonthica in my sorghum crop?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the weed of your sorghum, and you should pull it out at harvest. First, sow a sorghum variety that matures in 55-75 days when the soil is still short of rain. About two weeks after sowing do the first weeding to keep the field tidy. Then at the tillering stage, about 30-45 days after sowing, pull out the weeds so the crop does not have to compete for them. Do not use the same seed treat for Striga, because the fungicide treats a different problem. If you later see stunted plants or a dead-heart, go to ICAT for help.

history.content: My sorghum has Striga, it must be nutrient deficiency, so I just add fertilizer

draws.answer: It is not Striga, it is nitrogen washed into the seed. Striga appears as a purple-bracken rosette effect on the lower leaves, while nitrogen washed in does not start there and shows no spots. Because it is the washed-in kind, you must cut the striga plants at ground level and bury them, then grow a cereal right after. Plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field. When the sorghum is 20-25 days old, do the first weeding and apply NPK at 150-200 kg/ha, then earth up against lodging. Keep the second weeding and the foliar application of NPK at 50-100 kg/ha at panicle initiation. For matching the legume to your sorghum variety, see ICAT.

It is not nutrient deficiency, it is Striga, the parasite that grows on the straw planet around the base of the sorghum and pulls the root from the plant. Nutrient deficiency shows as a uniform pale yellowing of the older lower leaves while the young top leaves stay greener, in a pattern that spreads evenly with each season, and it is a deficiency of nitrogen, not a disease that a fertilizer alone can treat. To control Striga, cut the Striga stems at ground level and toss them into the soil, and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same plot for the second season. history.content: I see a pink-flowered weed clinging to the base of my sorghum and the plants look short. What should I do?

draws.answer: The weed is striga and you should use a striga-tolerant sorghum variety, sow it when the rains are strong, and perform the first weeding without delay. First, check whether striga is present; if you find it, plant a striga tolerant sorghum variety. Then, before sowing, take groundnut leaves and dry them over a pan. Mix about 2.5 kg of the groundnut leaf powder with 25 L of water and mix it well, then use about 20 kg of the mixture to give your field about 1.25 ha. After that, sow a sorghum extra-early variety (60-65 days) and perform the first weeding about 10 days after sowing. For a tolerant variety, contact ICAT.

history.content: how stop Striga seed buildup

draws.answer: Tight rows of maize are the condition that lets Striga form, so you first sow your maize on a rich, well-drained soil and follow the close spacing rule to keep the rows narrow. Then, when you plant, do the first weeding just like you would for a second crop, because the weeds that emerged after the first will compete with the stalks for nutrients. After that, sow a cereal right after the maize and cut the straw at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing roots stay in the soil. In the south, where the rains come in two seasons, ask ICAT for the calendar that fits your area, and in the north, where there is a single season, follow the advice of the long-term variety you chose.

Remove or bury all weeds in and around the maize plot at the weeding stage. Striga grows in the rows left by early weeding, so the weeds you pull are the ones that can sit and spread. After that, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the same field and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. If you later see striga in a field, go to ITRA or a registered producer and obtain the right tolerant variety.

history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink-flowered weed at the base, how can I manage it?

draws.answer: The pink-flowered Striga, known locally as the groundsel, must be removed before sorghum flowers. First, sow sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five grains per pocket at a depth of three to five centimetres and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. At two to three weeks after sowing, thin the seedlings to two or three plants per pocket and perform the first weeding without breaking the ridges. After weeding, apply the NPK fertilizer at one-hundred-fifty to two-hundred kilograms per hectare, then add urea at half the recommended dose, and earth up against lodging. For a targeted Striga attack, see ICAT.

The pink-flowered Striga plant that grows on sorghum is a parasitic weed that makes the sorghum stunted and you should pull it before the sorghum flowers. First, identify the sorghum striga clinging to the base of the base of stunted plants; this is the parasitic weed that makes them grow mottled and short. Then pull the striga plant out immediately. Next, sow a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field to use the nitrogen the striga takes from the soil. When you plant sorghum, create a small pocket in the sorghum rows and place the legume seed, making sure it is not too close to the sorghum stem. If you have any doubt about the striga problem, ask ICAT for help.

history.content: Would mixing two different insecticides give a stronger spray?

draws.answer: No. Insecticides are not mixed as products; a stronger product does not kill more pests, and mixing can make cleaning up far harder and leave residues on food. The rule for sprays is one application per layer, timed according to the product and the stage of the crop. Wash the plant before spraying, and make sure children and animals do not be near the sprayed area. If a crop is badly attacked, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

history.content: My sheep are dying fast from a disease that looks like PPR, what steps save the rest?

draws.answer: Your sheep are likely suffering from leucaena poisoning. Limit leucaena to only a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it be the main feed. Cut back the leucaena and mix it with grasses and cereal crop residues for adequate roughage. Change the feed composition slowly over several days. Ensure the animals always have clean water and a source of mineral or salt. If the sheep keep dying, see the veterinary service.

It is leucaena poisoning caused by mimosine building up from leucaena. First cut the leucaena back so it constitutes only a quarter to a third of the ration and never the main feed. Then mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen enough roughage. Introduce this new mix gradually over several days, while always ensuring clean water and a mineral or salt source are available. If the sheep keep dying and you cannot cut the leucaena back, see the veterinary service.

history.content: My sorghum is stunted and I notice a pink-flowered plant wrapping its stems near the ground. How can I manage this?

draws.answer: Pink-flowered, stunted sorghum shows a plant that is short and thin, and it has a high demand for nitrogen in the soil. First, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide because they cannot make a stunted plant improve. Second, bring organic matter back to the soil by using manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Third, add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Fourth, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot before any large purchase.

The pink-flowered plant is a sign of the parasitic weed Thedelia rubra. Pull out and destroy the severely affected plants that host the weed. Then, for the next season, plant a cereal and cut the stems at ground level to stop the thistles from remaining in the field. After that, sow a legume such as cowpea or soybean and cut the stems at ground level as well. Do not grow sorghum on the same plot for more than two consecutive years. history.content: How much urea should I mix with manure to control Striga on my sorghum?

When sorghum flowering begins, apply urea at 150 to 200 kilograms per hectare, then weed at 15 to 25 days and again at 40 days after sowing. Do not exceed the recommended nitrogen amount to avoid burning the plant. If you need a soil-specific adjustment, visit ICAT.

history.content: My field has some cassava with twisted leaves and others with brown rot inside the roots. Which problem am I dealing with?

draws.answer: I see you have cassava with twisted leaves and some with brown rot inside the roots. Those signs point to cassava mosaic disease, not bacterial blight. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and will feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation, never from mottled or deformed stems. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

Cassava browning of the roots is cassava bacterial blight, while cassava mosaic disease shows yellow mottling, stunted growth and leaf deformation, not root rot. First, pull out and destroy any cassava plants that have angular water-soaked spots, wilting young leaves or gum on the stem. Then, for the next sowing, disinfect your tools between each plant. Take cuttings only from plants that have no symptoms and plant them. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot to reduce disease pressure. history.content: I found a pink flower weed hugging the bottom of my short sorghum stalks, what steps should I take?

draws.answer: The pink-flowered Striga, known locally as zanguerati, is the weed that climbs into the stem of a sorghum plant and prevents it from bearing a stem. You should pull the Striga plant right away once you see it. After pulling the Striga, make sure to sow a sorghum variety that matures in 55 to 75 days and perform the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. This action stops the Striga from keeping the sorghum from flowering and dropping pods. For any sorghum questions, visit ICAT.

The pink-flowered Striga is the weed that attaches itself to the base of short sorghum and must be pulled at harvest. First, cut the sorghum stems at ground level and keep the young roots. Then, use a pinch to pull out a portion of the Striga plant that is clinging to the base. Remember that the same area must be cleared of all sorghum weeds before the next season. history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink weed clinging to its base, how can I fix this?

draws.answer: The problem is stalk borer on your sorghum and you must act quickly. While the sorghum is still young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel. Never apply neem powder by itself because the oil will scorch the plant; always use the sand or clay carrier. One kilogram of this mixture will treat about 1,500 to 2,000 plants, so use enough for your whole field. After the sorghum harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large block is attacked at once, go to ICAT for approved control.

The problem is groundnut rosette on your sorghum and no spray will cure the infection. Begin by roguing out any plants that are severely stunted and destroying them. Then, plant your sorghum early and use the recommended close spacing because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the sorghum field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that transmit the virus. Choose a tolerant sorghum variety for the next season. You can obtain resistant varieties from ICAT.

history.content: How do I manage an outbreak of peste des petits ruminants in my flock?

draws.answer: Peste des petits ruminants is called "cattle tick borne disease". First, keep your cattle well fed and watered so they can withstand the disease and recover. Second, stop moving, selling or gifting any animal in the sick herd. Third, isolate every surviving animal from any that showed signs. Fourth, do not move, sell or give any service to a sick animal. Fifth, vaccinate the entire herd with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, and repeat the vaccination on the recommended schedule. If you need help, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately.

Because the disease has no medicine that cures it, you must focus on isolating, vaccinating and controlling mosquitoes. history.content: There are purple flowers on weeds near my sorghum rows, what should I do right now?

draws.answer: The purple-flowered Striga, also called Althea, is the parasitic weed that grows on sorghum and is the only plant that benefits from the sorghum. Remove the purple Striga from the base of each sorghum plant before it flowers. Sow your sorghum on time and use the recommended close spacing so the stand becomes dense. When the plants reach tillering, pull out the purple Striga from the base and keep the sorghum close to the roots. For the following season, plant a sorghum variety that tolerates Striga. If you need help with the sorghum variety, see ICAT.

history.content: I have sorghum that stays short and yellow, and a purple weed clings to its base, what is the cause?

draws.answer: Your sorghum is suffering from nitrogen loss because the short, dense early plants are being pushed down by the purple-leafing Striga plant. Begin by pulling the Striga weed from each sorghum plant at the early stage. After that, sow a cereal crop in the same field and cut the straw at ground level to keep the residual nitrogen available. Do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide because they will not resolve the nitrogen shortage. After these actions, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper fertilizer dose for your plot.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: This is a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the urine colour because red-black urine points to redwater and yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

It is leucaena poisoning caused by feeding too much leucaena. Cut the leucaena back so it is only about a quarter to a third of the ration and never the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen gets plenty of roughage. Change the feed gradually over several days, and always keep clean water and a mineral or salt source available. If appetite does not recover, or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, see the veterinary service.

history.content: My goats are dying fast, they have fever, runny eyes and noses, and some have mouth sores, what is the problem?

draws.answer: The signs point to a tick-borne disease affecting your goats: gall sickness, which is anaplasmosis, or redwater, which is babesiosis. Both are parasites of the red blood cells carried by ticks, and they destroy red cells, which is why the gums, the mucous membranes and the mucous in the eyes go dry. Call the veterinary service the same day, because only they can identify the disease and give the correct drug and its dose; I will not give a drug or a dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown but never red points to gall sickness, and the two are not treated the same. Keep the sick goat in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick one.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the weed that appears between the roots of sorghum during the first month after sowing. First, sow sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Two to three weeks after sowing, apply the first weeding to keep unchecked weeds away. Then, when the two-row sorghum becomes two to three months old, treat each seed with 200 grams of NPK fertilizer and apply urea at 100 grams per hectare. Weed the sorghum at about fifteen days after sowing and again at two weeks. To resolve Striga, go to ICAT for a resistant variety.

Striga, also called sorghum striga, is the plant that grows between the roots of a sorghum stem and its young leaves, and it is what makes the crop grow poorly. First, sow a sorghum variety that matures in 55 to 75 days and plant it when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. Then carry out the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. When the plants reach tillering, about 30 to 35 days after sowing, pull out the striga plants with the stems removed. Finally, plant a sorghum variety that matures in 80 to 90 days, such as Sotubaka, and do the weeding on schedule. If you need help choosing the right striga tolerant variety, go to ICAT.
